speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the outlook for inflation and cost of living in 2023; (b) what are the key drivers; and (c) whether there is further scope to reduce imported inflation with a stronger Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Speaker, Singapore’s inflation outlook this year is dependent on both external and domestic factors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Externally, global inflation is likely to stay firm in the near term as global energy and food commodity prices remain elevated despite coming off their peaks in 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: At the same time, labour markets in advanced economies remain tight, thereby keeping pressure on wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Domestically, businesses are likely to continue to pass through elevated import and utilities costs, along with rising labour costs, to consumer prices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Meanwhile, housing rent and car inflation are projected to remain firm due to the strong demand for rental housing and tight COE quotas respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: On our monetary policy, as I had explained to this House in November last year, the effects of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)’s five successive monetary policy tightening moves will continue to dampen inflation in the year ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: MAS remains watchful of the near-term risks to inflation and growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The agency will review our monetary policy in April 2023.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I appreciate the proactive move by the MAS with the stronger Singapore dollar to help mitigate the imported inflation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have also read about how the supply chain has stabilised, which hopefully, will not add new pressures to our inflation from external sources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I wish to ask the Minister of State how much inflationary pressure does he see coming from domestic sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, how much of the inflationary pressure is domestically driven?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On domestic inflation, domestic inflation is related to external factors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, if you look at the external front, you might have fresh shocks to global commodity prices such as those arising from worsening geopolitical tensions or a significant strengthening of demand following the reopening of China's economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This, naturally, will result in higher domestic inflation, particularly for food and energy-related items.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Domestically, more persistent than projected manpower shortages could culminate in stronger labour cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government is aware of this but we expect this current tightness in the domestic labour market to ease over the course of the year, particularly with labour demand likely to soften amidst global economic headwinds, while continued non-resident inflows could also help to reduce labour market tightness and moderate cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government will look into the business environment and assess if more support schemes are required to support our businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just want to ask a broad, macro question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I have a sense of the Government's view of the growth and inflation bias for 2023 and into 2024 as well, especially with China reopening.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister of State has given a very extensive answer on inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But may I have a rough sense, what is the growth and inflation bias in terms of the outlook for 2023 and going into 2024?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why, for example, for the monetary policy to be proactive, for fiscal policy to be also supporting both our businesses as well as Singaporeans as a whole.
